blocks.text: 1. Corrective RAG (CRAG)

blocks.alt: Retrieved chunks go through a grader to be judged correct, ambiguous, or incorrect

blocks.text: Modular RAG established that patterns like this one are implemented as specific module combinations. Corrective RAG, or CRAG, grades retrieved chunks and corrects a poor retrieval, making it the first concrete member of the advanced RAG family covered in this module.
It scores each retrieved chunk and reacts differently based on that score, a grading and branching technique explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Grading Retrieved Chunks By Relevance

blocks.alt: A chunk goes through a grader to produce a relevance score

blocks.text: Unlike Naive RAG, which applies no grading to the retrieved chunks, a lightweight relevance grader scores each retrieved chunk as correct, ambiguous, or incorrect.
This simple three way classification drives what happens next.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Grade","What it means"],"rows":[["Correct","Chunk is relevant, proceed to generation"],["Ambiguous","Chunk is partially relevant, needs refinement"],["Incorrect","Chunk is not relevant, fall back to web search"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Correct When Retrieval Scores High

blocks.alt: A high score means using retrieved chunks as-is

blocks.text: When every retrieved chunk grades as correct, retrieval quality is already good.
The pipeline then proceeds straight to generation, exactly like naive RAG.
4. Incorrect Triggers A Web Search Fallback

blocks.alt: A low score or incorrect result triggers a web search fallback

blocks.text: When the retrieved chunks grade as incorrect, the local retrieval has failed.
CRAG falls back to an external web search instead of trusting the poor local retrieval.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A retrieval that grades as incorrect means the local knowledge base likely does not cover the question, making an external web search a more useful next step than forcing an answer from irrelevant chunks.

blocks.text: 5. Ambiguous Triggers Refinement

blocks.alt: An ambiguous score triggers a refine and retry step

blocks.text: When the retrieved chunks grade as ambiguous, they are only partially relevant.
CRAG refines the chunks by decomposing and filtering them rather than discarding or fully trusting them.
6. The Grader Is Its Own Small Model
Similar to the cross-encoder used in re-ranking, the relevance grader is typically a smaller, cheaper model than the main generator.
This keeps the added grading step relatively lightweight.
7. Grading Adds Latency To Every Query

blocks.alt: CRAG adds an extra grading step to every query

blocks.text: As Advanced RAG covers, each added step costs latency, and every single query now pays for a grading pass.
Even queries where retrieval was already fine still incur that cost.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pipeline","Extra cost per query"],"rows":[["Naive RAG","No grading step, lowest latency"],["Corrective RAG","One grading pass on every query, even successful ones"]]}

blocks.text: 8. CRAG Versus Self-RAG
CRAG grades the retrieved chunks specifically, while self-RAG, covered next in this module, reflects more broadly on the whole generation process.
These are two different forms of self-correction, one narrower and one broader.
9. Recognizing When Corrective RAG Earns Its Added Grading Cost

blocks.alt: Retrieval quality varying a lot points toward corrective RAG

blocks.text: A knowledge base with real coverage gaps benefits from a fallback path.
A knowledge base with consistently strong coverage, by contrast, rarely needs the fallback.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Using an expensive grading model when a lightweight one would work just as well.
Forgetting the web search fallback, leaving the pipeline stuck with only poor local chunks.
Applying corrective grading to every query even when the knowledge base rarely has gaps.
Treating an ambiguous grade the same as an incorrect one instead of refining it.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Corrective RAG grades retrieved chunks as correct, ambiguous, or incorrect and reacts accordingly.
A correct grade proceeds straight to generation just like naive RAG.
An incorrect grade falls back to an external web search rather than trusting poor local retrieval.
An ambiguous grade triggers refinement, decomposing and filtering the chunk rather than discarding it.
The relevance grader is typically a smaller, cheaper model than the main generator.
Grading adds latency to every query, even ones where retrieval was already fine.
CRAG grades retrieval specifically, while self-RAG reflects more broadly on generation.
Corrective RAG earns its cost most on knowledge bases with real coverage gaps.
Next up: Self-RAG, covering broader self-reflection across the whole generation process.
